passage: Counsellor's note, Nirmala. Tenzin came to see me after the third weekend of working. The boss praises Tenzin's dedication in every meeting, "our most reliable person," and each time hands over another project. Tenzin laughed while describing this, but the laugh was thin, and Tenzin's eyes were red. I can't tell how much is tiredness and how much is worry about saying no. Together we made a two-week log of tasks and hours. Then Tenzin drafted a short list of priorities, with the items that could wait, to take to the boss on Monday, plus one plain sentence: "I can do A or B this week, which matters more?" We agreed that health comes before praise. I'll see Tenzin again next Friday.

qa.q: What did Tenzin and Nirmala make together?
qa.a: They made a two-week log of tasks and hours.

qa.q: What might Tenzin be feeling, given the thin laugh and red eyes?
qa.a: Probably tiredness and worry about saying no, though Nirmala admits the balance is unclear.

qa.q: What could Tenzin say when the boss hands over another task?
qa.a: "I can do A or B this week, which matters more?", along with the list of priorities and the log of hours.

qa.q: How might the boss see Tenzin's heavy workload?
qa.a: Possibly as a reward for reliability, and the boss may not notice the load it creates.

grounding: A boss praises dedication and piles on more; documenting workload, proposing priorities and being ready to say no.

passage:
Day one. Madhuri, Seema's manager, stopped at her desk. "You're so dependable. Can you take the Delhi client too? Nobody else could handle it." Seema said yes and felt proud.

Day twelve. Seema now had four accounts; her colleagues had two each. Her back hurt, she was eating dinner at ten, and Madhuri had just added a fifth. "You never let me down," Madhuri said. Seema smiled and felt something sink.

Day twenty. Seema spent a weekend morning writing it down: every account, hours worked, deadlines missed by others that she'd covered. She brought it to Madhuri with a list. "These are my priorities. I can do three accounts properly. Which two should move?"

Madhuri looked surprised, then flipped through the pages. "I didn't realise. Let's move the Delhi one and the new one."

Seema walked back to her desk, legs shaky. Saying no had been terrifying. It had also worked.

qa.q: How many accounts did Seema's colleagues have by day twelve?
What was Seema feeling on day twelve when Madhuri added a fifth account?
qa.a: She felt a sinking dread and exhaustion behind her smile, since her reliability was only bringing more work.

qa.q: What did Seema do on day twenty, and why did it work?
qa.a: She documented her workload and proposed priorities, asking which accounts should move, which made the overload clear and let her say no.

qa.q: How does Madhuri see Seema's workload at first?
qa.a: Madhuri sees Seema as dependable and doesn't notice the pile-up until she sees the written list.

grounding: Over several weeks, the passage shows a boss who praises dedication and piles on more, and a young woman who documents her workload, proposes priorities and says no.

passage:
"Reena, you keep saying yes to your boss. Let me tell you about my first job.

I, Sonali, was twenty-four, at a bank in Bhubaneswar. My manager called me 'our rock.' Every time I finished something, he gave me two more. 'You're so reliable,' he'd say, and I felt so proud. I was there till nine every night. I got headaches every day.

Then one evening I fainted on the bus home. The conductor had to call my father.

That frightened me into doing what I should have done earlier. I wrote down everything on my desk and the hours I worked, and I took it to my manager. I said, 'I can do these three well. Which ones go to someone else?'

He was angry for a day. Then he moved the work.

Don't wait for the bus, beta. Being reliable doesn't mean saying yes to everything."

qa.q: What did the manager call Sonali?
What did Sonali feel when the manager praised that reliability?
qa.a: Sonali felt proud at first, even as the extra work brought daily headaches.

qa.q: What turning point in Sonali's story led to action, and what was done?
qa.a: Fainting on the bus frightened Sonali into documenting the workload and asking the manager which tasks to move.

qa.q: How might the manager have seen Sonali's list?
qa.a: He was angry for a day, perhaps because he had relied on Sonali taking everything, but then accepted it and moved the work.

grounding: An elder recalls a boss who praised their reliability while piling on more, and how they documented the workload and proposed priorities after their health suffered.
